units.title: Unit 09 — Everyday verbs 3
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 22–23 (PDF pages 26–27).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Everyday verbs · have, take and pay
learningObjectives: Use have with experiences, conversations and activities, rather than substituting make or get.
Choose take naturally in travel, risk, interest and action expressions.
Use pay in fixed collocations and recognise the formality of paying tribute or respects.
Distinguish alternative verb–noun combinations and choose forms suitable for natural British English.

items.example: Drivers can have an accident even on a familiar road.
items.note: Have an accident describes experiencing an accident, not making one.

items.example: We sometimes have an argument about household chores.
items.note: An argument here is a disagreement, not a logical argument in an essay.

items.example: I would rather talk calmly than have a row over money.
items.note: Informal, especially British English, for an angry argument; row rhymes with cow.

items.example: We usually have a break halfway through the workshop.
items.note: Have a break is a normal choice for stopping work or study briefly.

items.example: Could we have a conversation about the project timeline?
items.note: A neutral expression for talking together, usually for more than a few words.

items.example: We can have a chat after the conference.
items.note: More informal than have a conversation; have a chat with someone is a common pattern.

items.example: Some visitors have difficulty understanding the local accent.
items.note: Use have difficulty doing something, normally without a before difficulty.

items.example: After a long day, I sometimes have a dream about flying.
items.note: Have a dream can refer to a dream during sleep; it can also refer to a personal ambition.

items.example: I sometimes have a nightmare after watching a horror film.
items.note: A nightmare is a frightening dream; have, not make, is the usual verb.

items.pt: passar por uma experiência; ter uma experiência
items.example: You may have an experience abroad that changes your perspective.
items.note: Use have an experience to refer to something you live through; it can be positive or negative.

items.example: I have a feeling that the meeting will finish early.
items.note: Often followed by that and a clause to introduce an intuition rather than a proven fact.

items.example: You can have fun at the festival without spending much money.
items.note: Have fun is the standard verb phrase; make fun of someone means ridicule them.

items.example: I hope you have a good time at the reunion.
items.note: A natural alternative to have fun, particularly about an event or period spent somewhere.

items.example: Could you have a look at this diagram before I print it?
items.note: Usually followed by at to name what is examined; take a look is also natural.

items.pt: dar uma festa; fazer uma festa
items.example: We are going to have a party to celebrate the new office.
items.note: Have a party refers to organising or enjoying a social gathering.

items.example: Please tell me if you have a problem with the booking.
items.note: Commonly followed by with; have a problem and have problems are both natural.

items.pt: ter problemas com; ter dificuldades com
items.example: They sometimes have problems with the online payment system.
items.note: The plural is useful for recurring or multiple difficulties; with introduces the issue.

items.example: Would you like to have a try at the new simulator?
items.note: Informal invitation to attempt an activity; have a go has a very similar meaning.

items.example: Everyone should have a go at solving the puzzle.
items.note: Informal, especially British English; often followed by at and a noun or -ing verb.

items.pt: tirar férias; fazer uma viagem de férias
items.example: We hope to take a holiday somewhere quiet next spring.
items.note: Take a holiday is natural for going on a break from work or daily routine.

items.pt: fazer uma viagem; dar um passeio
items.example: We plan to take a trip to the coast next month.
items.note: Take a trip is common for travelling somewhere, often for a relatively short visit.

items.example: Visitors can take a train directly to the city centre.
items.note: Take a train names the means of transport; get the train is also heard in British English.

items.example: You can take a bus from the airport to the university.
items.note: Use take a bus for using bus transport; take the bus is equally common.

items.pt: passar a gostar de; simpatizar com
items.example: I quickly took a liking to the small seaside town.
items.note: Means begin to like someone or something, often quite quickly or unexpectedly.

items.example: You take a risk whenever you ignore a safety warning.
items.note: Take a risk is the standard combination for doing something with an uncertain outcome.

items.example: She began to take an interest in local history.
items.note: Often means develop or show active curiosity about a subject or person.

items.example: Tourists often take photos of the old railway station.
items.note: Take photos is more natural than make photos in general British English.

items.example: I decided to take a chance and apply for the scholarship.
items.note: Often suggests trying something despite uncertainty, especially when there may be a benefit.

items.pt: passar a não gostar de; criar antipatia por
items.example: He seemed to take a dislike to the new policy immediately.
items.note: Means develop a negative feeling about someone or something; compare take a liking to.

items.example: Students should take advantage of the free language workshops.
items.note: Usually means make good use of an opportunity; it can also mean exploit a person unfairly.

items.example: The council must take action to repair the unsafe bridge.
items.note: Take action is the usual combination for doing something to address a situation.

items.example: Please pay attention to the instructions before starting.
items.note: Pay attention to is standard; have attention is not a natural replacement.

items.example: It is kind to pay a compliment when someone has done good work.
items.note: Pay someone a compliment means say something positive about them; not make a compliment.

items.example: You can pay your last respects at the memorial service.
items.note: Usually used for showing respect to someone who has died, at a funeral or memorial.

items.pt: prestar homenagem a; reconhecer publicamente o mérito de
items.example: The director will pay tribute to the volunteers during the ceremony.
items.note: Rather formal; often refers to publicly honouring their work or achievements.

items.example: We want to pay a surprise visit to our former teacher.
items.note: Pay a visit to is a conventional, slightly formal alternative to visit; surprise specifies the kind of visit.

sectionsChecked: A · Have: experiences, conversations, difficulties and activities
B · Take: travel, photos, interests, risk and action
C · Pay: attention, compliments, respects and tribute
Usage differences, register and verb selection

units.title: Unit 10 — Synonyms and confusable words 1
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 24–25 (PDF pages 28–29).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Synonyms and confusable words · restricted partners
learningObjectives: Select close/shut, start/begin, big/large and end/finish according to the noun and meaning.
Distinguish old, ancient, antique and elderly, and expressions for being alone or feeling lonely.
Choose charge/load, injure/damage and grow/raise with their characteristic objects.
Correct typical learner errors while preserving differences in register and meaning.

items.section: A · Close, shut, start and begin
items.example: The chair will close the meeting after the final vote.
items.note: We normally close a meeting, conference or discussion rather than shut it.

items.section: A · Close, shut, start and begin
items.example: The organisers will close the conference with a short speech.
items.note: Close is conventional for formally bringing an organised event to an end.

items.section: A · Close, shut, start and begin
items.example: Please close your mouth slowly after the examination.
items.note: A neutral, polite choice in contexts such as a dentist appointment.

items.section: A · Close, shut, start and begin
items.example: It was upsetting to hear the manager say, "Shut your mouth," to an employee.
items.note: An impolite or confrontational command; avoid it when asking someone to be quiet politely.

items.pt: dar partida em um carro; ligar um carro
items.section: A · Close, shut, start and begin
items.example: It can be difficult to start a car when its battery is flat.
items.note: Start is the normal verb for making an engine run; begin a car is incorrect.

items.pt: dar partida em um motor; ligar um motor
items.section: A · Close, shut, start and begin
items.example: Always check the area is clear before you start an engine.
items.note: Start, rather than begin, collocates with engines and vehicles.

items.pt: o universo começou; o universo teve início
items.section: A · Close, shut, start and begin
items.example: Scientists continue to investigate how the universe began.
items.note: Begin is preferred in some formal or abstract contexts; started is possible in other contexts, but less typical here.

items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: Choosing a new career can be a big decision.
items.note: Big here means significant or important, not physically large.

items.pt: um grande problema; um problema sério
items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: A lack of reliable data could become a big problem.
items.note: Big commonly expresses the seriousness of a problem; large problem is less idiomatic in this meaning.

items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: This jacket is available in a large size.
items.note: Large is conventional as a clothing size label; big size is generally unnatural.

items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: They agreed to end their relationship amicably.
items.note: End means decide to stop an ongoing relationship; finish is less natural here.

items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: A film ends with the mystery still unsolved.
items.note: End describes how a story or event concludes; finish can refer to completing an activity.

items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: You should finish your homework before dinner.
items.note: Finish means complete a task; end your homework is not the usual choice.

items.pt: terminar de escrever uma redação; concluir uma redação
items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: I hope to finish an essay before the deadline.
items.note: Finish stresses completing the writing; end an essay refers to how its content concludes.

items.pt: concluir uma redação; encerrar um texto
items.section: A · Big, large, end and finish
items.example: You can end an essay with a brief summary of your argument.
items.note: End focuses on the final part or closing words, not necessarily on completing the whole task.

items.pt: um velho amigo; um amigo de longa data
items.example: I met an old friend at the station by chance.
items.note: Old friend can mean someone known for many years, not necessarily an elderly person.

items.example: The museum occupies an old building near the harbour.
items.note: Old is a general description of age; ancient suggests a much earlier historical period.

items.example: She chose ancient history as her main subject.
items.note: Ancient modifies history relating to early civilisations; antique history is incorrect.

items.example: In ancient times, many goods travelled along trade routes.
items.note: A set combination for a distant historical period.

items.pt: móveis antigos de valor; mobiliário de antiquário
items.example: The shop specialises in antique furniture from Europe.
items.note: Antique commonly describes valuable old objects, not people or historical periods.

items.pt: joias antigas de valor; joias de antiquário
items.example: She inherited some antique jewellery from her grandmother.
items.note: Antique is appropriate for collectible older objects; elderly jewellery is incorrect.

items.example: An elderly person may need extra time to board the bus.
items.note: Elderly is a generally polite adjective for older people; do not use antique for people.

items.example: She moved closer to home to help her elderly parents.
items.note: Elderly commonly modifies people; old parents is possible but may sound less considerate.

items.pt: mãe solo; pai solo; responsável sem parceiro
items.example: A single parent may have to balance work and childcare.
items.note: Single parent means a parent raising a child without a partner; it does not mean an only parent.

items.pt: um lugar isolado; um lugar solitário
items.example: They found a lonely place in the mountains to camp.
items.note: Lonely can describe a remote location, as well as the feeling of lacking company.

items.example: New students may feel desperately lonely during their first week.
items.note: Desperately intensifies lonely, describing strong feelings of isolation.

items.example: Many adults choose to live alone in the city.
items.note: Alone means without another person; lonely describes an emotional state and is not interchangeable.

items.example: She prefers to travel alone when visiting museums.
items.note: Alone describes travelling without companions and does not necessarily mean feeling lonely.

items.pt: uma figura solitária; uma pessoa isolada
items.example: A solitary figure waited at the empty bus stop.
items.note: Literary or descriptive: a single person seen apart from others.

items.pt: o único sobrevivente; a única sobrevivente
items.example: The sole survivor was rescued the following morning.
items.note: Sole emphasises that there was exactly one survivor.

items.example: Growing up as an only child does not mean you always feel lonely.
items.note: Only child is the normal expression for a person without siblings; single child is not the usual term.

items.pt: uma ocasião única; um acontecimento excepcional
items.example: The reunion was a unique occasion for the former students.
items.note: Unique describes something exceptional or without an equivalent; not simply a solitary person.

items.example: Remember to charge your phone before a long journey.
items.note: Charge is used for adding electrical energy to a device or battery, not load.

items.example: You should charge a battery according to the instructions provided by its manufacturer.
items.note: Charge is the conventional verb for replenishing battery energy.

items.example: The workers will load a lorry with building materials.
items.note: Load means put cargo into or onto a vehicle; British English lorry means truck.

items.pt: carregar uma van; colocar carga em um furgão
items.example: The crew will load a van with the equipment after lunch.
items.note: Load refers to putting cargo into a van; charging an electric van refers to adding energy to its battery.

items.example: Workers were preparing to load a ship at the port.
items.note: Load a ship means put cargo aboard it, not charge its batteries.

items.pt: carregar uma arma de fogo com munição
items.example: A safety instructor explained why nobody should load a gun without authorisation.
items.note: Load a gun means put ammunition into it; charge a gun is not the standard combination.

items.example: Volunteers helped injured people reach medical care.
items.note: Injured refers to people or animals with physical injuries; damaged describes objects.

items.pt: machucar uma perna; lesionar uma perna
items.example: You can injure a leg if you fall awkwardly.
items.note: Injure is used for harm to people or parts of the body; compare damage a chair.

items.example: The shop offered a discount on a damaged sofa.
items.note: Damaged normally describes things, not injured people.

items.example: Farmers in the region grow crops suited to dry weather.
items.note: Grow is typically used with crops and plants, rather than raise.

items.example: It is possible to grow plants in a small flat.
items.note: Grow plants is the conventional expression for cultivating vegetation.

items.example: Some farms raise cattle on large areas of grassland.
items.note: Raise collocates with farm animals and children; grow cattle is incorrect.

items.example: Parents can raise children in many different kinds of family.
items.note: Raise children means bring them up; grow children is not the normal phrase.

items.example: They raise sheep on a small hillside farm.
items.note: Raise is conventional for rearing animals; grow sheep is incorrect.

items.section: D · Big and large: dictionary extensions
items.example: Better lighting made a big difference to the room.
items.note: Big can signal significance, not simply dimensions; large difference is also possible in quantified contexts.

items.section: D · Big and large: dictionary extensions
items.example: Getting the contract was a big deal for the small firm.
items.note: Informal way to describe something important; not generally interchangeable with a large deal.

items.pt: um grande número; uma quantidade elevada
items.section: D · Big and large: dictionary extensions
items.example: A large number of visitors attended the exhibition.
items.note: Large number is a conventional quantitative expression; big number has different, more informal uses.

items.section: D · Big and large: dictionary extensions
items.example: A large survey examined commuting habits across the country.
items.note: Large can refer to the scale of a study; the meaning differs from the important sense of big.
